segments.narration: A B-24 sat intact in the Sahara for fifteen years. Found in 1958, 710 kilometres inland from the Libyan airfield it flew out of.
Guns still loaded. Radio still working. A thermos of tea somebody could have drunk. And not one person aboard, not one parachute.
April 1943. First mission, bombing Naples. Coming home in the dark, they flew straight over their own base and never saw its flares.
Their direction finder couldn't tell a bearing from its exact reverse. So they kept going south for two hours, certain the desert below was sea.
Eight survived the jump and walked north. Five made 130 kilometres. One made over 320. The ninth man was never found.

verdicts.claim: The B-24D Lady Be Good was located in the Libyan desert in 1958, about 710 kilometres southeast of its base at Soluch, and was remarkably well preserved.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: sighted from the air 16 May 1958, reported by a BP team 9 November 1958, reached on the ground 27 February 1959 at 710 km (440 mi) southeast of Soluch. The narration's 'found in 1958' matches the year of discovery; ground confirmation was 1959.

verdicts.claim: The wreck still held working machine guns, a radio, food and water, and a drinkable thermos of tea, with no human remains or parachutes aboard.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: machine guns, radio and some food and water still aboard, a thermos of tea was drinkable, no human remains or parachutes found at the wreck.

verdicts.claim: The crew's only mission, on 4 April 1943, targeted the harbour of Naples, and on the return they overflew their own base without seeing the flares fired to guide them in.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: nine-man crew flew their first mission together 4 April 1943, target Naples harbour, took off 14:15, reached Naples 19:50; the crew overflew their base apparently without seeing the flares fired to guide them in.

verdicts.claim: The base's single-loop direction finder could not distinguish a bearing from its reciprocal, so the crew flew about two hours south believing they were still over the Mediterranean.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: the base's direction finder used a single loop antenna which could not distinguish a reciprocal bearing; the crew flew south for about two hours believing they were over the Mediterranean, bailing out at 02:00.

verdicts.claim: Five crewmen were found in February 1960 about 130 kilometres north of the crash site, Harold Ripslinger over 320 kilometres away, and Vernon Moore was never officially found.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia: five bodies found 11 February 1960 about 130 km (81 mi) north of the crash site; Ripslinger found over 320 km (200 mi) from it; Vernon Moore has never been officially found. Woravka's parachute failed, so eight survived the jump.
